items.title: Khabib Nurmagomedov: Dagestan, MMA, UFC, Islam, Conor, Fedor & Football | Lex Fridman Podcast #500
items.transcript_text: - The following is a conversation with Khabib Nurmagomedov, one of the greatest fighters of all time, who retired from the UFC undefeated with a perfect twenty-nine and O record. It was a huge honor for me to meet him, to train together, and to have this deep conversation. We had this conversation entirely in Russian. This was my first time doing so on this podcast. And even these words I'm saying right now are spoken in Russian. So if you're hearing me in English, you're actually listening to the English dub. On YouTube, you can switch between language audio tracks by clicking the settings gear icon, then clicking audio track, and then selecting the language you prefer. For the original Russian version, select Russian. And for the English dub, select English. Subtitles are also available in both languages. The translation and dubbing are a collaborative effort of translators, real human beings, including myself and AI. Thanks to the incredible team at ElevenLabs for their help. And now, please allow me to take this moment to say thank you from the bottom of my heart for your love and support all these years. I love you all. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. And now, dear friends, here's Khabib Nurmagomedov. Let's try in Russian if we can, like you suggested. - I can help you out if you need. - Yeah, thanks, brother. I kind of feel it in my heart and soul, but sometimes I can't find the right words. - I know, brother. We got this. - Great. Let's start from the beginning. So that gym back in Dagestan where you trained is legendary for its spartan conditions. There was just one shower for seventy people, only cold water. And yet, this humble little gym managed to raise more than twenty world champions, including several UFC champions. Can you try to explain or maybe reflect on what factors in that gym, those training sessions, that life in Dagestan created so many champions? - Sure. So we're talking about the gym, the one located in Makhachkala. And Makhachkala, for the people who don't know, it's the capital of Dagestan. This was back around the years from two thousand to two thousand and ten, and even later on. In twenty nineteen, we opened up a big gym, a major facility that is still functioning to this day. But before twenty nineteen, we all actually trained in that gym where there was practically nothing. It was just a school gym with nothing but mats, a single punching bag, one climbing rope, and a kind of indoor basketball court. And if we go even further back, before two thousand, before we moved to Makhachkala, we lived in a village. In the village, we had a gym right inside our house. My father, he built a gym at home, and he was training all the local village kids right there. And there were times back when I was a child, let's say when I was maybe six or seven years old, I would occasionally wake up to the sound of, people training, doing their drills right there in the gym. You know, like with judo or freestyle when they're drilling, one guy throwing another. Those are my first conscious memories. I was maybe five, six, seven years old at that time. So my father set up this gym in the village and trained local kids, including me, my older brother, and all our close and distant relatives, anyone who wanted to come. A lot of kids came to him. - So you would wake up and there are these sounds. - Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You hear the hitting, the throwing over and over. And my father's voice, how he's shouting, giving instructions, pushing someone, coaching, teaching. I lived with those sounds. But that was in the village. And later when we moved to Makhachkala, well, you couldn't say the gym there was wow either. There were only mats. And of course, the most valuable thing an athlete can have, a coach, my father. So he trained us there. And to be honest, let's say, until I became a champion and had big success, we never had a good big gym where we could, you know, all take a shower together at the same time after training. We always had just one shower for everyone, no proper amenities. - So your life story began in the mountains of Dagestan in Sildi, then Kirovaul, and then Makhachkala. And in all these situations, there are very interesting stories. But one of the things I heard you say is that the best results are born out of the worst conditions. What can you say about that? Philosophically, is it correct to say that comfort is kind of the enemy for champions? - It depends on the sport. For example, let's say in football, you have to have conditions. You can't really play if there is practically no field. Of course, you can play in the dirt, and it happens sometimes. You can start there. But when you are ten or twelve years old, you already have to be at a certain level. You must have conditions. But if we look at our sport, then what is the most important thing? The coach. You also need sparring partners who will push you in the gym, as they say, right? And you need the mats. Our sport is not expensive. You just buy your wrestling shoes, singlets, shorts, a T-shirt. And if there's a mat, you wrestle, you become a champion, you fight. But when you live too well, let's say, you know, you're never in need. For example, you were born into a wealthy family and you already have everything. Would that same wealthy father, would he force you to do such a brutal sport? A sport where you come home every day with injuries where you come home with an exhausted body, you come home with bruises. Would he really do that? That's the question. And the kid himself, who lives a life of luxury, would he even want to do this? When we look at it statistically, the answer is no. This is where you need that hunger. You have to be in a position where you are truly in need. - And it's interesting that there's a psychological side to this as well, that you need a tough situation to create champions. But what's really interesting is how Dagestan has produced so many wrestling champions. You mentioned football. Let's look at other countries. Why has Brazil produced so many great football players? Why does Argentina have so many football players? Of course, you have Germany, France, and all that. - European, yeah. - The whole European side. But those are completely different cultures. - Yes. Well, in Brazil, their strength is in their numbers. How many people do they have? The population is huge, more than two hundred million. And people really love it there. It's a huge tradition. Because, you know, without a real love for this sport, you can never achieve any success. You truly have to love what you are doing. So they have the tradition and they have the love for it, and that is why they play for all the top clubs. Well, I think they just win by numbers. - Yeah, that's a powerful aspect of their culture. How much people, how much the whole nation loves to play football. And if you add to that a system that creates strong teams, that's how you can produce so many football legends. - Yes. Take Dagestan, for example. We love football. I just know how much people in Dagestan love football. Yes, we have wrestlers, fighters. There are many of us. But for football players, there is no ecosystem like that. Not so well organized where a kid can, for example, play at school, then go to some academy, then get noticed there, and then get picked up by a club. We don't have that system. It's just kids running on the streets, playing on the streets, following football. Let's say playing on PlayStation. There is no system. There is no selection process where kids can go and show themselves, so they can be noticed and get signed. I think Brazil and other countries, and of course Europe, they have it. So yeah, we have big problems with football. However, in our sports where you can, where you can wrestle, where you can fight, in that sense, we have a system. For example, the gyms, you know, in Makhachkala, let's say for combat sports. I'm not even counting like freestyle wrestling or other styles. There may be forty or fifty gyms for combat sports, and all are full. If you win in Dagestan, you move on to the North Caucasus level, then to the Russian nationals. If you're champion of Russia, you go to the Worlds. In amateurs, they notice you and you make a name for yourself. There is a certain ladder here. But in many other sports here in Dagestan, we don't have such a well-structured ladder for people to climb. - Can we look at this philosophically again? I mean, you've seen so many wrestlers, fighters. Why exactly were these gyms creating so many champions? I'm just honestly curious because it's rare in any sport, one gym or a small number of gyms creating so many champions. - Well, first important factor is the competition level is incredibly high. You come to the gym, and in every spot you have good wrestlers, ten or fifteen guys right there, and the coaches are great. You know, it so happened that my father broke through in the media, and then I became a champion, and the other guys became champions too. And my father's philosophy, it really resonated, and he became known for it. But there are coaches in Dagestan that not many people know about. They are known locally, but they are very good, and actually they have the knowledge, they have the approach, they have the philosophy. They could also be at the same level as my father was. I believe there are really quite a few of them. In terms of the coaching, I think Dagestan was extremely lucky. It probably goes back to the nineteen fifties when wrestling really took off here, starting with Ali Aliyev, our legendary wrestler, a five-time world champion who went to the Olympics three times. That's where it started, with his generation. There was Zagalav Abdulbekov, Ali Aliyev. Those are the well-known names. I mean, those guys are famous, but there were so many other less known wrestlers who later on, after they retired, they all became great coaches themselves. And these coaches, they raised a very large number of guys who are really good at wrestling. And then some of those coaches, they kind of switched over to fighting, let's say to grappling, to MMA, and they started coaching in combat Sambo as well. And it just kept going like that, you know. It was moving forward step by step. And so we have a huge number of really great coaches. I believe this is one of the single most important keys to the success of Dagestani wrestlers and fighters, the coaching staff of Dagestan. - Is it more about technique or is it really just about serious, incredibly hard work? - Well, you have to look at the traditions, because generally it's just the way it is in Dagestan. Everyone wrestles. Everyone fights. It's part of our culture. You know yourself, fighting is like fifty percent wrestling. Every parent wants their children to wrestle, to be physically strong. Our approach to kids is that a child must be strong. They must be able to stand up for themselves, for their family. It's something that has traditionally always been in every single one of our clans, every family, every village. It's just in our blood. - I mean, it's worth pointing out, and you've actually written about this, that this isn't just a recent thing. It's been going on for hundreds of years. - Yes, that's right. These lands, Dagestan specifically, have seen powerful armies sweep through time and time again. Because of that, people here have always had to fight to survive. - Refusing to back down, refusing to give up their land or lose their identity. - Their homes, their villages, yeah, their families, and land. If we look back a thousand years in history, maybe fifteen hundred years, there was the Khazar Khaganate, the Arabic Caliphate, then the Iranian Empire, or the Persian Empire, I should say. Then the Russian Empire, Timur passed through there, the Mongols. And if we look at the geographical location of Dagestan, for those who don't know, the Caucasus range runs across the whole region like a wall, and then it slopes down right where the Caspian lowlands are. So you've got the sea on the right, the mountains on the left, and the Caspian lowlands right here. And there was a city there that's still standing today. It's one of the oldest cities in the world, not just in Russia. It's Derbent. It used to be called Babul Abwab. It means the gate of gates. Very major trade routes went through there. Very large armies passed through, and it was bound to leave a mark on the people. we have so many languages, more than thirty different languages, and people just don't understand each other. Take Islam and me. We have different languages, come from different backgrounds. Islam is Lak, and I'm Avar. When we talk, it's not like it's a dialect. We don't understand each other at all. But since Islam has been with us for nearly twenty-five years, he actually picked up some Avar over time. But anyway, the deep history of the region, it all left its mark. It created many different languages and traditions. Basically, of course, Islam is our primary religion, but Dagestan has actually absorbed a lot of cultures and faiths. Even our food culture, it is incredibly rich. We have European and Asian and Caucasian, our own unique cuisine. So on the people, on the people themselves, the last fifteen hundred years of history have left a huge mark. If you're into history and you start reading about Dagestan, I think you'll get completely immersed and be amazed by what a unique place it is. So all of this left a huge mark. Look at the terrain. It's a coastal plain, and then the mountains rise up. For instance, take someone like Timur. When he passed through with a huge army, he stayed in the Dagestan lowlands but never went up into the mountains. Why? Because you've got hundreds of thousands of troops, soldiers traveling with horses and supplies. If they had started going up into the mountains where it's cold and there are no roads, it would have been too tough for them. So the highlanders somehow managed to stay independent. But the lowlands, the Caspian lowlands of Dagestan, they kept changing hands. Massive empires would roll in, and all of that left a mark on the people. Gate of the gates, Babul Abwab. Historians wrote about it, say, a thousand or fifteen hundred years ago, great historians from various countries. People have written so much about Dagestan. It went by different names back then, but they wrote a ton about this exact region. Many people, many empires invaded our land. - So do you feel that inside you, in your blood, your heart, like all of this history? - Well, in the past, it's not like I really felt it. I knew Dagestan's history, but maybe with time, you start to see it in a whole new light. Every year, you change a bit on a mental and psychological level. Now I understand. I really do. You cannot just be born physically and mentally strong. Your environment shapes you no matter what, where you grew up, how you grew up, the conditions, and who you had around you. And after all, genetics are also a part of who you are. So when you add all this up, yeah, I just feel like all of this has come together inside me. - It's interesting because in sports, we know many of the names of the great fighters and wrestlers. Yet when it comes to war, there are so many people who fought, heroes, truly great warriors. Some we know by name, but most of them we'll never actually know and- - We'll never know. - You write about Imam Shamil, that he's an important figure for this region and a hero as well. - Well, Imam Shamil, he was known for resisting an empire as huge as Russia. Dagestan is so small, and he had so few people with him. How did he get famous? He got famous because he held out for a very long time. He didn't just resist for a couple of years. He was like a regular fighter, let's say, a soldier for ten years, and then when he became the leader, he went on for another twenty-five years. So, 35 years of his conscious life he spent fighting not just some random empire, but what was then, if not the most powerful, definitely one of the strongest empires of that era. And that is what made him famous. And so there are villages in Dagestan that deeply honor the memory of particular warriors who came from their villages, from their clan, from their ethnic group. But in, well world history, they're barely known. Like, take Shamil. He's a leader, right? So everybody knows him. But there are plenty of heroes who've been forgotten. But yeah, their own people remember. - Villages hold on to history. Plus, we have to admit that conditions in the mountains are incredibly harsh. That's part of it too. Just surviving up there is a real struggle. - See, back then, people in the mountains worked all through the summer just to survive the winter, because winters are harsh, with heavy snow, completely cutting off villages. People just stay inside and try to outlast it. And in the summer, they work. Terrace farming was a huge thing for us. Our terraces are among the most, you could say, famous and ancient in the world. They're known as the Chokh terraces. Now, those are the famous ones. But every village had terraces. There's a place out there called Marghit, right across from our village. People worked over there, but here, in the village, is where they lived. I mean, you'd think, why didn't they just build a village right there, in the place where we grow all our food? Because enemies could easily ride in on horseback. An army could easily get to you there, so they'd build a village in rugged terrain- ... somewhere tough to invade. For instance, our village is Sildi. It's from the word si, which is like a castle or a fortress or a tower. They built it that way so an army couldn't reach them. You'd have to hike down one mountain and then climb up a whole different mountain. And right there, they'd plant things like grain, potatoes, basically, you know, all their food. See, if we had built over there, if we lived there and grew our crops in the same place, since it's all terraced land, an army could just walk right up, launch raids, and so on. Back in the day, that's how people lived. And so all of this took a toll on people, physically, psychologically, and mentally. And honestly, well, you just can't be born in these conditions, live here, stay here, and be mentally weak. You just have to be tough. There's no other way to survive. - So you just built a sports complex there. Pretty legendary, you know. Could you talk about that? - Yes, that was my father's whole plan. He really wanted it way up in the mountains. First, it's great for the fighters. Right now, I just flew out here to Las Vegas. We're sitting here, like, doing this podcast together, but I came out here for Umar's fight. And I should say, Umar did his main training there at the new base in Sildi. He spent almost a month at that place. And because it's 1500 to 1600 meters above sea level, man, it's tough to train there. And And the thing is, when you spend about three to four weeks there, you just have more oxygen in your blood, you have more testosterone, you improve physically, you know, your stamina builds up, and so on. And what if you didn't have any thoughts at all? What if you couldn't think, couldn't understand anything? These thoughts, this awareness, your mind, your abilities, none of that was there before. Then it appeared. Why? That's the question. None of us existed. Then we were born. We were little. We weren't aware of anything. We didn't remember anything. Then little by little, we grew up and became adults. We became successful, became somebody. We became who we are. So why did all of this come specifically to you? There are so many questions like that. And so these questions are, let's say, a kind of guide through life. And for me that's what religion is. It guides me and helps me. - You often say, "Alhamdulillah, all praise to God." That's very powerful, that sense of gratitude. Can you tell us, can you explain why you say it so often? - You know the saying, the tongue speaks what the heart is full of. The way you speak shows what's in your heart. If you have something dark in your heart, your words will show it, no doubt. We all have some dark parts in our hearts. Every single person has them. Sometimes they come out in what we say, how we express ourselves, what we share with people, and so on. Everyone has that. But if your heart is mostly good and pure, then that will also be reflected in your speech. And And I just like praising the Almighty and giving all the credit for my success back to Him because everything we have is given to us by the Almighty. Throughout the history, there have been many people who made big mistakes after becoming successful, powerful, and wealthy, and they started saying, "No, no, this happened to me because I'm so great, because I'm so, I'm so intelligent, because I had vision, because I've got the brains, because I'm extremely capable. That's why all of this came my way." But at the same time, there were many others who worked just as hard, who weren't any less intelligent, and the Almighty just didn't give it to them. He chose you and gave it to you, and you just have to give the credit back to Him. You shouldn't take the credit for yourself. That's what I believe. And it's something I've come to through studying my religion. I understand that everything the Almighty has given to me is not because of who I am. It's simply something God has given me as a test to test me and, in the end, see which of my deeds outweigh the others, the good or the bad. Because as a believer, I believe that there will be judgment and everything we have, everything we do, every action we take, we will be held accountable for it. There will be a day of judgment, there will be scales, and everything will be weighed. - What advice would you give young people about life and their careers? Millions of people are watching you and deeply respect you. What would you say about how to live your life? And how do you find your path and stay on it? - Well, I wouldn't want to speak just from my own perspective. I'd rather bring people back to the scripture, to what the Almighty said, "Read." That's the first word revealed in the Holy Quran. The first command is read or ikra. So to everyone listening to or watching this podcast, I would want to bring them back to that. Read, meaning what? Educate yourself, observe, learn, improve, but don't stay in one place. And anything a person is truly looking for, if they genuinely want to find it, not just find an answer, but find the truth, they can reach it, but they can never reach it without reading. They need to read. When a person reads, what they read enters them into their body, their heart, their mind, and it triggers a search. A search for knowledge begins inside them, but if you don't read, you won't find anything. Just listening to someone is one thing, but reading is something different. So my advice would be read and find within yourself the strength to come closer to one God and seek to understand why we were sent here in the first place. Today, you and me, we're almost the same age. So let's just think about this. For example, my grandfather on my mother's side passed away in two thousand and three. Now it's twenty twenty-six. He's been lying in the grave for twenty-three years. And then there was his grandfather, or let's say his great-grandfather who also died and has been in the grave for over a hundred years, roughly speaking. But what about people who died two thousand years ago? They've been in the grave for two thousand years. What's next? It's a good question, isn't it? They've just been in the grave all this time, and that's it. So what was the purpose of their life? A person has been in the grave for two thousand years, but maybe lived for seventy years. Roughly speaking, let's say one hundred. They lived for one hundred years and have been in the grave for two thousand. So what matters more, those one hundred years or these two thousand years? And what happens after those two thousand years end? People believe different things, whether there is a day of judgment or not. That's where the difference lies between a believer and a non-believer. After everyone is resurrected, there will be the day of judgment. There will be judgment, and after that, people will enter eternity. Eternity compared to eternity, what are two thousand years? They're nothing. And we live for, let's say, seventy years. And many people choose those seventy years over eternal life. And if a person understands that these seventy years they have here, roughly speaking, seventy or eighty years are meant to be used to prepare for what comes after, so that when the day of judgment arrives, and after that judgment they can live forever, not in hell, but in heaven. If that becomes their ultimate goal, then they will strive to do good deeds because they will fear the day of judgment. And that's really what life is about, preparing yourself for the day of judgment. - That's true. To truly understand life and its deeper meaning, you have to think about eternity. Only then can you really understand your role. - Actually, it can keep a person away from evil. From evil and, and it can stop them from treating other people badly. It can hold a person back. But if you don't have that understanding, if a person lives completely convinced that there's nothing after death, what's there to stop him from doing evil? Just like that. What do you think? And on top of that, an even more dangerous combination. You become powerful, wealthy, and you become famous. What now? Suddenly every door is open to you. Just imagine a person like that. And on top of all that, he doesn't believe in the day of judgment. He doesn't believe he'll be held accountable for his actions. That's, you know, it's like a nuclear bomb. He can end up causing harm to people everywhere. But if you know that for everything you have here, you'll eventually have to answer, that there will be a day of judgment and that you'll be called to account, and if you fail that test, you'll burn in hell forever. That'll make you rein yourself in a little. You'll have to take that into consideration. You'll have to tighten things up a little. You'll begin to understand that you're not nearly as important as the image you've created of yourself in your own mind. You start becoming more, as Americans say, down to earth. You become more grounded. You're not flying, you're walking on the ground. - You once put it beautifully. You can allow money and fame to stay in your hand, but not in your heart. You've still got many years ahead of you, but you're already an example of someone who's become famous, made money, and remained the same person. - If money stays in your hands and not in your heart That's a good thing. But the moment it gets into a person's heart, it corrupts them. Once it's there, it's very difficult to pull it out of your heart. If you have wealth in your hands and use it properly for good causes, for the right purposes, for people in need, for your family, relatives, friends, people from your hometown, that's a good thing. But as soon as that wealth gets into your heart, it becomes very difficult to share it with others. And this is a very dangerous place for a person to end up. And I'm sorry, but as a believer, I believe that most people in hell will be wealthy. - One of the reasons millions of people find you so interesting to watch is that you're constantly growing. First, you were a great fighter. Now you're becoming a leader. Your wisdom just keeps increasing. You're evolving as a person, but still the core values remain. It's good to see, inspiring for people. Money and fame haven't changed you. You're just growing as a human being, as you always have. - I hope it's in the right direction. It's just, the thing is people only see the good. They don't see the bad. And we all have the good side and the bad side. Everyone, sadly. And especially when it comes to celebrities, we only show the best side of ourselves. Even when you post photos, you only post the good ones, the pictures where you look your best. So I hope that the way people see me, as you pointed out, is the way I really am, because it's difficult to judge yourself objectively. You're always biased when it comes to yourself. That's how it is. We tend to think highly of ourselves, right? You can't really see yourself objectively. We hide our flaws and put our best qualities on display. Sometimes people even start believing in a fake version of themselves. For me, I try to stay on the honest path throughout my life to remain true to who I really am and to show my true self to people. Maybe not everyone agrees with my behavior, my opinions, my worldview, or my attitudes toward, towards sports, religion, and other things. Not everyone shares my views. Not everyone is a fan of mine. There are people who, let's say, see me very differently. So I'm just... I've tried, I continue to try to be who I am. That's all. And I hope that my ending will be a good one, too. Well, you know, at least that's my hope. - You've stayed the same, but you've also grown. I mean, today you even managed to say something nice about Barça. So see, that's progress. Yeah. Well done. - Come on, without Barcelona, there wouldn't be Real Madrid. If the Spanish league didn't have either Real Madrid or Barcelona, it just wouldn't be the same. They've been competing against each other for how many years? One hundred twenty. It's hard to imagine Barcelona and Real Madrid without each other, and so is the Spanish league without that rivalry. It's impossible to imagine. So yeah, we have to give you some credit, but Real Madrid is the royal club. Come on. It's the best. You know? - And thanks to both of them, we've been able to enjoy truly incredible football for so many years. - For so many years, yeah. - Um, Khabib, brother, I don't even have the words to explain how honored I am that you're here talking with me today and showing me so much warmth. There's no way to fully express what you mean to millions of your fans around the world, including me. Thank you so much for everything. Thank you for this conversation. - Thank you. Thank you very much, Lex. - Thank you for listening to this conversation with Khabib Nurmagomedov. And again, thank you for everything. I love you all. Goodbye, my friends. See you next time.

items.title: Gary Gallagher: American Civil War, Slavery, Lincoln, Grant & Lee | Lex Fridman Podcast #499
items.transcript_text:
- You cannot control what a great military event can set loose. More battle casualties than US forces had suffered in every war combined down to that point happened in two days. Two and a half months after that, George B. McClellan's army engaged with Lee's army in what came to be called the Seven Days Battles at Richmond, 36,000 casualties. So those two together just showed that this was gonna be on a totally different scale. He added a psychological twist. What, what Grant envisioned his doing, and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia, is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and then Sherman did it in Georgia. But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically. I'm gonna show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." The great forces are all that matters and individuals don't really matter notion of history I think is ridiculous. Individuals really matter. For the United States, Lincoln and Grant matter beyond calculation- ... in this war. And on the Confederate side, if you take Lee out of the picture, the war doesn't last nearly as long as it does. In terms of causation, if you take slavery out of the picture, there is no Civil War, period. - The following is a conversation with Gary Gallagher, a historian of the American Civil War. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here's Gary Gallagher. The American Civil War broke out in 1861. What were the causes of the Civil War? Could it have been avoided, or was it inevitable? - I don't know if anything is inevitable in history, but it's certainly safe to say that the conditions were in place to make it possible- ... by the winter of 1860, '61, and the conditions that made it possible were all related to the institution of slavery and its effects both in the states where slavery was allowed and the states where it was not allowed. And there had been a series of tensions that grew in the decade preceding the 1850s. It's not that one side wants to get rid of slavery and the other side wants to protect slavery. I'm talking about the white people in the United States now who would be making the political decisions. It's a question of whether slavery was going to be able to expand into federal territories. That is what really created the starkest difference between the two sections in the 1850s, even in the late 1840s. The issues that came to most, uh, perilous a point in the view of many people then had to do with whether slavery would be allowed only where it already existed, or would it be allowed to expand. If it could expand, then it seemed that it might be conceivable at some point even that the slaveholding states could end up with a majority. They were in a minority by 1860, '61 and feeling beleaguered, feeling threatened. They'd long since lost the population race to the free states. Early in the nation, the most powerful states were slaveholding states. Virginia was by far the most important state. Four of the first five presidents were from Virginia, all slaveholders, all prominent members of the slaveholding class. Those days were long gone by the late 1850s. - So that's an important thing to say. It wasn't before the Civil War a discussion about abolishing slavery. It's about whether slavery, the institution of slavery should be expanded. - Allowed to expand into federal territories. There, there is a portion of the white population that is adamantly in favor of getting rid of slavery immediately. The abolitionists, they... There was even a political party called the Liberty Party, that ran a candidate in 1840 and they got a handful of thousand votes. They reached their high point in 1844. They got about two and a half percent of the vote. The abolitionists are a tiny minority among the— even in the North, tiny minority among the white people of the United States. The African American population, nearly four million of them by 1860, of course, would have embraced it instantly and yearned for it. But in the white population, the abolitionists are a tiny minority. They are much despised even across much of the North because they were seen as agitators who roiled the Union and deepened rifts that might bring a significant political break. - So how did this escalate to a civil war, this almost policy discussion about the institution of slavery? How did it actually escalate? - It escalated into a civil war because in the presidential election of 1860... There'd been two party systems in the United States. The first party system, the Republicans, the Jeffersonian Republicans versus the Federalists. After that, there was, the two parties were the Whig Party against the Democratic Party. The Democratic Party grew out of the Jeffersonian Republican Party. It's the same party. The Whig Party foundered to a significant degree on the issue of slavery. How do you maintain a national party that has a wing in the Southern states and has a wing in the Northern free states that can handle the issue of slavery? The Democrats managed to do that. The Whigs could not do it, and so the Whig Party ran their last candidate in 1852, presidential candidate, significant candidate. And the Republican Party emerged in the mid-1850s, took most of the old Whigs into the Republican ranks and one of the Republican, the key Republican platform plank was no expansion of slavery into the territories. Not abolish slavery, no expansion. That was the key in 1856 when they ran their first candidate. In 1860, that is again the key plank in the Republican platform. The Republican platform in 1860 says where slavery exists it will continue, but it cannot expand into the territories. When white Southerners saw that, that meant that they were doomed to become an increasingly minority section in the nation, and you would have a federal government increasingly dominated by the free states that could then do the one thing that the white South could not countenance, and that is tamper with the institution of slavery in the South. The presidential election of 1860 brought the destruction of the last national party, which was the Democrats. They couldn't even settle on a candidate, so you end up with a Northern Democratic candidate running, Stephen A. Douglas, and a Southern candidate running. The convention fractured and John C. Breckinridge ran on the, on the Southern Democrat platform. You had a Unionist candidate running who just didn't wanna talk about slavery, let's talk about the Union, and you had Lincoln running as a Republican. When Lincoln won, the white South looked at Lincoln winning. Here's a guy who has said that he doesn't think slavery would expand, but he'd said more than that. He scared the white South more because in 1858, both Lincoln and William Henry Seward, these are two prominent, prominent Republicans, had said basically in separate speeches, the House Divided Speech on Lincoln's part, the Irrepressible Conflict Speech on Seward's part, that the nation could not continue in the long term half slave and half free. And everybody in the South knew which way they wanted it to be. They would want it to be no slavery. And so Lincoln's election scared the white South enough so that seven of the 15 slave-holding states seceded in response to Lincoln's election. They seceded between December 20th, when South Carolina went out, and the end of February. You had the deep South went out. - What was the general view amongst the populace towards slavery? Let's kind of lay it out. Let's you know, for the audience looking back, let's put ourselves in the mind space of how people saw the world, how people saw slavery, how people saw African Americans. - Well, the baseline among the white Americans, there were about 31, shade more than 31 million Americans in 1860 for the census of 1860. About four million of them were African Americans, three and a half million of those enslaved in the South. Anyway, among the white population, the average attitude toward Black people is what we would call profoundly prejudiced. Doesn't matter whether you... A lot of people think this is a Southern white thing. They're the only ones who were prejudiced. By our standards, the overwhelming majority of people in the free states were also deeply prejudiced. It's important to keep in mind that attitudes towards slavery and attitudes toward race do not, they're not necessarily the same. I mean, you could be against slavery and still be prejudiced against Black people. By our standards, many abolitionists were prejudiced against Black people. They... But the overwhelming majority of the white North, in the North, often had a hard time getting my students to understand the demographics in 1860. The free states in 1860 were more than 98% white. 98% white. African Americans are a tiny minority in the free states. Black people lived in the 15 slaveholding states in 1860. Most of the white North, by our standards, was very prejudiced. They were against the expansion of slavery into the territories because they thought that would circumscribe white opportunities to make an economic life in these federal territories, and they didn't want that to happen. About 45% of the people who lived in the free states were Democrats. Most Democrats had no problem with slavery. I mean, absolutely no problem with the institution of slavery. There would be more problems among Republicans, especially with extension of slavery, although many Democrats, white Democrats in the North were against that as well. The white South was overwhelmingly in favor of slavery. You often read the argument, the kind of neo-Confederate argument that they'll talk about how most Confederate soldiers didn't own slaves. That's true. The a large majority of families in the South did not own a single slave. But all white Southerners had a stake in slavery. They had a stake in it as a form of labor control, but more important than that, they had a stake in it as a means of social control. They knew, no matter what they said later in the Jim Crow era of how happy Black people were in the institution of slavery, they knew that Black people, of course, did not want to be enslaved, and they were afraid of what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore. They had in the backs of their minds Haiti. Is that what's gonna... If you live in one of the coastal districts of South Carolina where 90% of the residents are enslaved and you're a white person, you probably don't sleep all that soundly at night if you think there's any chance that the Black people are not gonna remain under the control of the white people. So all white people in the South had a stake in slavery, not just some. All of them did, and there were all kinds of ways that it would go back and forth. If you were a modest farmer and grew a little bit of cotton, you didn't have your own cotton gin, you... but your more wealthy neighbor had a gin, could gin your cotton there, and then you would take your turn on the slave patrol, the slave patrols. So there's a reciprocity in that regard. - This is perhaps a bit outside the scope of what we'll talk about today, but just to lay out the context on slavery in general in human history, we should say that slavery was ubiquitous. It existed in virtually every major civilization in the history of humans. Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, North and South America. We should also say something that, as I was looking into this, another big topic, which is the Atlantic slave trade. And it was surprising to me, the stat I wasn't aware of, I would venture to say most Americans probably don't know, that only 4% of African slaves were brought to North America, to the United States. - Brazil is the main destination. - Brazil, the Caribbean was over 90%, 4.9 million in Brazil, 4 million in the Caribbean, and it was also the last of the Americas to abolish the slave trade. So only 4% of the Atlantic slave trade went to the United States. So there's-- the story of human slavery is one that reaches deep into our history and geographically is much larger than we often study in the context of the United States. - One thing the war, the Civil War, which I'll just call the war for the rest of our discussion, I mean, one thing it did was end slavery in four years in the United States. Whereas in the absence of that war, it might have gone on for decades. I think the United States would have had the ignominious distinction of being the last place to get rid of slavery, would have been after Brazil, would have been after Spanish Cuba, because it was thriving in the United States in 1860. It was making the transition from cash crop agriculture- ... to other, to industrial applications and other applications growing of non-- not growing, growing just cotton and rice and sugar. It was-- There was a time in the literature when people argued that the war was needless, the Civil War was needless because slavery was on its way out. That's absolutely wrong. It was not on its way out. It was thriving. Lincoln said at one point he thought it might have lasted another fifty years, and I don't know how many years it would have lasted, but I think it would have lasted longer than it did in either Cuba or Brazil if it hadn't, if the war hadn't taken place. - So slavery was flourishing in the United States from- - Flourishing. - ... from an economics perspective- ... especially. - The wealthiest part... The 1860 census is our friend, and it tells us that the people who controlled the most wealth in the United States were slaveholders, and their property in slaves alone, not their other holdings, not their land holdings, just property in slaves were valued at about three billion dollars. The value of all industries, all railroads, all of that put together, fewer than two point five billion dollars. So the people who controlled the most wealth, by far, were the slaveholding class. - So it was the most valuable industry in the United States, and perhaps it is the reason, Again, a bit out of scope, but maybe it helps lay out the land. Let's look at the nineteenth century. So most slave-owning societies of the era were able to abolish slavery without people dying at the mass scale that we'll discuss. So Britain freed eight hundred thousand slaves in 1833- ... By buying their freedom. Russia freed twenty-three million serfs in 1861 with a decree, so legally. Brazil, which imported more than ten times as many enslaved Africans as the United States, abolished slavery in 1888 through basic ordinary legislation. No violence. Why did the US have a civil war with an estimated seven hundred and fifty thousand people dead in order to abolish slavery? - Yes. That's-- Let's talk just for a second about the seven hundred and fifty thousand dead soldiers we're talking about. The number for years was six hundred and eighteen thousand, and that's been revised lately. I think we're probably certainly more than seven hundred thousand. By far the bloodiest war in, in our history as a percentage of the population off the charts, by far the bloodiest. I think there's a big difference between Great Britain doing it and the United States doing it, is Great Britain did it in other places. There weren't millions of enslaved people in Great Britain at the time. It's-- I think, for them, it might have been a little bit easier to free enslaved people who don't live among you than it... In the United States, the ante is up for the Confederacy because they, the enslaved people lived here, and I think they were, a lot of them were afraid of them and what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore. The war goes from... It doesn't begin as a war to end slavery. There's a major shift in the war, begins in the summer of 1862, where you add to the war. The war aim for the United States initially is to suppress the rebellion, which is what they called this. They didn't call it the Civil War for the most part during the war. It's the War of the Rebellion. That's the goal initially. As the war goes on and becomes costlier and more all-encompassing, they decide that they're not gonna be able to suppress the rebellion unless they also strike at slavery, because slavery underpins the Confederate war-making capacity. You have enslaved labor that keeps the economy going and allows the Confederacy to mobilize between eighty-five and ninety percent of all their white military-aged males. It's an astonishing mobilization. It's only possible because enslaved labor keeps the economy going. If you take that enslaved labor away, it deals a significant blow to the Confederate economy and, and by extension, to its ability to wage a nineteenth century war. - So the Emancipation Proclamation was in part a military strategy. - Abraham Lincoln based it entirely on his war-making power as commander-in-chief in a time of open rebellion. His inclination, there's no-- He's often been criticized for not including the soaring language he was capable of in the Emancipation Proclamation. One historian likened it to a bill of lading. It had all the soaring language of a bill of lading. He did that on purpose. He did it because he, he doesn't have the power to strike at slavery in the absence of a war. The president doesn't. And he did it because he knows that he can't win the war with only Republicans in the army. He needs to keep Democrats on board with the war as well. They're not in favor of emancipation. The one way that they might accept it is as a tool to help achieve union, and to do that we've got to strike at the rebels this way, strike at slavery. That will hurt their war effort, and it will also punish the people who brought on the war, and that would make... So Lincoln hoped that by basing it strictly on his war power, it might be more widely accepted across all parts of the loyal states and not as controversial as it was. It was still intensely controversial. It alienated many Democrats when he issued it, who said, "You're changing what this war is about. We're willing to shed our blood and maybe risk our lives to restore the union of the founders. I'm not gonna risk my life to free a Black person." That's a very, very common attitude among Democrats. - So what did the Emancipation Proclamation actually do? It emphasized the freeing of slaves in the South. - It's even more complicated than that. The only place that Lincoln said he had the power as the war leader to strike at slavery is where the rebels were actually still in rebellion and in control. So any place where the US Army was in control, any place-- He said that it is in essence United States territory now. I can't free them there because I don't have the power. I can only free them where we don't have the power. So he exempted parts of states and areas in the South that it didn't apply to as of the moment he signed it. Going forward, any place that the United States Army went where it hadn't been on January 1st, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation applied and enslaved people would be freed by it. At the, literally at the time he signed it, he didn't free anybody because he's only saying, "I can free them where we're not in control. We have to be in control for this to have effect and for this to have power." - So in part, this is why the army was the boundary which the freeing was happening. - It's, it's, it's absolutely the boundary, and Congress had already passed what was called the Second Confiscation Act. It passed this in July of 1862 that announced that all enslaved people belonging to rebels were free. It didn't apply to people who could prove they were unionists living in the South and owned slaves. Lincoln didn't make that distinction in the Emancipation Proclamation. His proclamation is broader than the Second Confiscation Act was. - Okay. There's so many tangents we can take, but let's zoom out once again. There's a difference between cause, as you've talked about, cause and motivation. - Absolutely. - Quite a large number of people volunteered to fight. - In fact, a majority of all the soldiers who fought on both sides were volunteers during the Civil War. About 3 million served, 2.2 million in the United States, 800, 900,000 in the Confederacy. It's, again, I talk about things that are hard to get students to understand. This is one of them. They have to separate... The causation and motivation are often conflated, and not just by students but also by lots of talking heads on newscasts in the United States who don't know anything about United States history- ... but know what they know. In terms of causation, if you take slavery out of the picture, there is no Civil War, period. That's not a long conversation you need. You ask the question. That's the answer. Let's go to the next question. The next question is, okay, so were most white people motivated to put on blue uniforms because they wanted to kill slavery? The answer to that is no, they were not. They were motivated to put on blue uniforms to salvage the Union, which they saw as a unique gift that the founding generation, based on the bloodshed in the American Revolution, had bequeathed the successive generations. And the two key parts of what the Union meant for them was, number one, you had a voice in your own government, and someone will always say now to me, "Well, but women couldn't vote." That's right. The people who could vote by our standards were limited in the 19th century, but within the context of the Western world in 1860, the United States had by far the broadest franchise, by far. And so they argued that's one thing the Union gives us, and it also gives us the chance to rise economically. Doesn't guarantee that you can succeed, but it means you're not doomed to be what your father was. And those are worth fighting for. And so I will put on a uniform so the slave-holding aristocrats and oligarchs, which is what they called them, of the South, they said they're not... They don't really believe in democracy. It's an oligarchy- ... in the South. It's a slavery-based oligarchy, and we know which way Europe's going, they said. The revolutions of the 1840s failed in Europe. Europe's going the wrong way. They're going toward more aristocracy, more oligarchy, more... And we are the last hope. When Lincoln spoke of the last best hope of Earth, which he did in one of his most memorable phrases, he's meaning that the United States is a beacon of small D democracy in a Western world that seems to be turning the other way. And those soldiers, it meant, it meant it was that important to them. They are citizens in a republic that people shed blood to establish, and we can't let it go.
